name: Information-highway rhetoric
description: Exploratory road and surfing metaphors used during public introduction of networked communication.
cause_of_death: Documented media decline and contemporaneous irritation with repeated transportation metaphors.

sources.title: What Happened to the Information Superhighway
sources.note: Contemporary Nexis counts show newspaper references dropping from 4562 in 1995 to 842 in 1999.

sources.title: Surfing the Internet: An Introduction Version 2.0.2
sources.note: Preserves Jean Armour Polly's contemporary nontechnical guide and its surfing metaphor.

sources.title: Where does the word cyber come from?
sources.note: Oxford Dictionaries retrospective distinguishes displaced affirmative formations from continuing security terminology.

sources.title: Merging Into Electronic Traffic on Superhighway Is Causing Some Anxiety
sources.note: Contemporary report records irritation with highway puns. Only short lexical fragments retained.

entries.gloss: An expansive network presented as a new route to information.

examples.text: Could you send those notes down the information superhighway?

entries.rationale: Nexis counts support a 1995 crest and steep decline by 1999; onset and 2001 fade are conservative curation estimates.

entries.surface: road kill on the information superhighway
entries.gloss: Being left behind or overwhelmed during network adoption.

examples.text: I need another day before this becomes road kill on the information superhighway.
road kill on the information superhighway

entries.rationale: The 1994 report directly records this already-irritating pun. The signature models its brief media moment, not a measured individual usage curve.

entries.gloss: Joining networked activity through a transportation metaphor.

examples.text: We are merging into electronic traffic; please circulate the agenda.

entries.rationale: Attested in a 1994 report about fatigue with network metaphors; peak and fade delimit that moment by inference.
